1: # Qt For Python
2: 
3: Qt For Python is the [Python Qt bindings project](https://wiki.qt.io/Qt_for_Python),
4: providing access to the complete Qt framework as well as to generator tools for
5: rapidly generating bindings for any C++ libraries.
6: 
7: Shiboken is the generator used to build the bindings.
8: 
9: See README.pyside6.md and README.shiboken6.md for details.
10: 
11: ## Building
12: 
13: To build both Shiboken and PySide simply execute:
14: 
15:  * `python setup.py build`, or
16:  * `python setup.py install`
17: 
18: to build and install into your current Python installation.
19: 
20: The same setup.py script is used to build all the components of the project:
21: 
22:  * shiboken6 (the supporting Python module)
23:  * shiboken6-generator (the bindings generation executable)
24:  * PySide6
25: 
26: Preferably, a Qt (build) environment should be used to automatically pick up
27: the associated `qtpaths6`, but optionally one can specify the location of `qtpaths6`
28: and `cmake` if it is not in the current PATH with:
29: 
30:  * `--qtpaths=/path/to/qt/bin/qtpaths6`, and
31:  * `--cmake=/path/to/bin/cmake`
32: 
33: respectively.
34: 
35: By default, all of the above is built when no special options are passed to the
36: script. You can use the `--build-type` parameter to specify which things should
37: be built:
38: 
39:  * `--build-type=shiboken6`, build/package only the python module
40:  * `--build-type=shiboken6-generator`, build/package the generator executable
41:  * `--build-type=pyside6`, build/package the PySide6 bindings.
42:  * `--build-type=all`, the implicit default to build all of the above
43: 
44: When building PySide6, optionally, one can specify the location of the
45: shiboken6 cmake config path if it is not on the current PATH with:
46: 
47:  * `--shiboken-config-dir=/path/to/shiboken/cmake/config/dir`
48: 
49: This is useful if you did a cmake installation of shiboken6 into a custom
50: location.
51: 
52: For Windows, if OpenSSL support is required, it's necessary to specify the
53: directory path that contains the OpenSSL shared libraries `libeay32.dll` and
54: `ssleay32.dll`, for example:
55: 
56: * `--openssl=C:\OpenSSL-Win64\bin`
57: 
58: This will make sure that the libraries are copied into the PySide6 package and
59: are found by the QtNetwork module.
60: 
61: ## Building Additional Options
62: 
63: On Linux and macOS you can use the option `--standalone` to embed Qt libraries
64: into the PySide6 package. The option does not affect Windows, because it is
65: used implicitly, i.e. all relevant DLLs have to be copied into the PySide6
66: package anyway, because there is no proper rpath support on the platform.
67: 
68: You can use the option `--rpath=/path/to/lib/path` to specify which rpath
69: values should be embedded into the PySide6 modules and shared libraries. This
70: overrides the automatically generated values when the option is not specified.
71: 
72: You can use the option `--qt-conf-prefix` to pass a path relative to the
73: PySide6 installed package, which will be embedded into an auto-generated
74: `qt.conf` registered in the Qt resource system. This path will serve as the
75: PrefixPath for QLibraryInfo, thus allowing to choose where Qt plugins should be
76: loaded from. This option overrides the usual prefix chosen by `--standalone`
77: option, or when building on Windows.
78: 
79: To temporarily disable registration of the internal `qt.conf` file, a new
80: environment variable called PYSIDE_DISABLE_INTERNAL_QT_CONF is introduced.
81: 
82: You should assign the integer "1" to disable the internal `qt.conf`, or "0" (or
83: leave empty) to keep using the internal `qt.conf` file.
84: 
85: ## Development Options
86: 
87: For development purposes the following options might be of use, when
88: using `setup.py build`:
89: 
90:  * `--ignore-git`, will skip the fetching and checkout steps for supermodule
91:    and all submodules.
92:  * `--limited-api=yes|no`, default yes if applicable. Set or clear the limited
93:    API flag.
94:  * `--module-subset`, allows for specifying the Qt modules to be built.
95:    A minimal set is: `--module-subset=Core,Gui,Test,Widgets`.
96:  * `--package-timestamp`, allows specifying the timestamp that will be used as
97:    part of the version number for a snapshot package.
98:    For example given `--package-timestamp=1529646276` the package version will
99:    be `5.x.y.dev1529646276`.
100:  * `--reuse-build`, option allows recompiling only the modified sources and not
101:    the whole world, shortening development iteration time.
102:  * `--sanitize-address`, will build the project with address sanitizer.
103:  * `--skip-cmake`, will reuse the already generated Makefiles (or equivalents),
104:    instead of invoking, CMake to update the Makefiles (note, CMake should be
105:    ran at least once to generate the files).
106:  * `--skip-docs`, skip the documentation generation.
107:  * `--skip-make-install`, will not run make install (or equivalent) for each
108:    module built.
109:  * `--skip-modules`, allows for specifying the Qt modules that will be skipped
110:    during the build process.
111:    For example: `--skip-modules=WebEngineCore,WebEngineWidgets`
112:  * `--skip-packaging`, will skip creation of the python package, enabled (Linux
113:    or macOS only).
114:  * `--verbose-build`, will output the compiler invocation with command line
115:    arguments, etc.
116:  * `--disable-pyi`, will suppress the generation of .pyi files. This allows
117:    debugging when the project builds but the pyi generator complains.
118: 
119: ## Requirements
120: 
121:  * Python 3.10+ is supported (for Qt 6.11+)
122:  * CMake: Specify the path to cmake with `--cmake` option or add cmake to the
123:    system path.
124:  * Qt 6.x is supported. Specify the path to qtpaths with `--qtpaths` option or
125:    add `qtpaths6` to the system path.
126: 
127: ### Optional
128: 
129: #### OpenSSL:
130: 
131: Specifying the `--openssl` option only affects Windows. It is a no-op for other
132: platforms.
133: 
134: Please note that official Windows packages do not ship the OpenSSL libraries
135: due to import/export restrictions as described in
136: https://doc.qt.io/qt-6/ssl.html#import-and-export-restrictions
137: 
138: You can specify the location of the OpenSSL DLLs with the following option:
139: `--openssl=</path/to/openssl/bin-directory>`.
140: 
141: You can download
142: [OpenSSL for Windows here](http://slproweb.com/products/Win32OpenSSL.html)
143: 
144: Official Qt packages do not link to the SSL library directly, but rather try to
145: find the library at runtime.
146: 
147: On Windows, official Qt builds will try to pick up OpenSSL libraries at
148: application path, system registry, or in the PATH environment variable.
149: 
150: On macOS, official Qt builds use SecureTransport (provided by OS) instead of
151: OpenSSL.
152: 
153: On Linux, official Qt builds will try to pick up the system OpenSSL library.
154: 
155: > **Note**: this means that Qt packages that directly link to the OpenSSL
156: > shared libraries, are not currently compatible with standalone PySide6
157: > packages.
158: 
159: #### macOS SDK:
160: 
161: You can specify which macOS SDK should be used for compilation with the option
162: `--macos-sysroot=</path/to/sdk>`, for example:
163: ```
164: --macos-sysroot=/Applications/Xcode.app/.../Developer/SDKs/MacOSX10.12.sdk/
165: ```
166: 
167: #### macOS minimum deployment target:
168: 
169: You can specify a custom macOS minimum deployment target with the option
170: `--macos-deployment-target=<value>`, for example:
171: ```
172: --macos-deployment-target=10.10
173: ```
174: 
175: If the option is not set, the minimum deployment target of the used Qt library
176: will be used instead. Thus it is not necessary to use the option without a good
177: reason.
178: 
179: If a new value is specified, it has to be higher or equal to both Python's and
180: Qt's minimum deployment targets.
181: 
182: Description: macOS allows specifying a minimum OS version on which a binary
183: will be able to run. This implies that an application can be built on a machine
184: with the latest macOS version installed, with latest Xcode version and SDK
185: version and the built application can still run on an older OS version.
186: 
187: 
188: ## CMake super project
189: 
190: For development convenience, a CMake super project is included in the root of
191: the repository.
192: 
193: The super project can be built using standalone CMake, or using an IDE's CMake
194: integration (Qt Creator for example).
195: 
196: Nevertheless the default build process is done via setup.py, in which case each
197: of the sub-projects are built and installed separately, as mentioned, the super
198: project is just for development convenience.
199: 
200: ## IDE (Qt Creator) case
201: 
202: When using an IDE, just open the root CMakeLists.txt file as a new project, and
203: make sure to specify the following things:
204: 
205:  * `LLVM_INSTALL_DIR`, the environment variable should point to your libclang
206:    library location
207:  * `Qt`, either select a Qt Kit when configuring the project, or make sure that
208:    the `qtpaths6` binary is present in the PATH environment variable.
209:  * `Python`, the PATH environment variable should also point to the Python
210:    interpreter which you wish to use for building the projects (can either be
211:    a system interpreter, or a virtualenv one for example)
212: 
213: Once that is done, just re-run CMake, so that it picks up the new environment
214: values. If needed, all other cache variables defined by the project files can
215: be re-adjusted (for example FORCE_LIMITED_API).
216: 
217: ## Command line CMake case
218: 
219: When building using the command line CMake binary, make sure to invoke it in
220: a separate build directory, and not in the root source directory.
221: 
222: Make sure you have the correct environment variables set up, as described in
223: the previous section.
224: 
225: The invocation would then look like:
226: ```bash
227: mkdir build && cd build
228: cmake -DCMAKE_BUILD_TYPE=Release ..
229: # ninja
230: ```

103:     # Append any existing ld_prefix values, so existing PATH, LD_LIBRARY_PATH, etc.

108:     if(WIN32)

112:         # Replace the CMake list separators with "\;"s, to avoid the PATH values being
113:         # interpreted as CMake list elements, we actually want to pass the whole string separated
114:         # by ";" to the command line.

118:         endif()

122:         if(env_value)

124:         endif()

132: def _prepare_designer_app(app_path: Path) -> Path:
133:     """Copy Designer.app to a temp dir, strip com.apple.provenance, re-sign
134:     ad-hoc, and return the binary path inside the prepared copy.
135: 
136:     Only called when com.apple.provenance is detected on the app bundle, which
137:     happens when Designer.app originates from an internet download (e.g. Qt
138:     installed via the Qt Maintenance Tool). The provenance attribute causes the
139:     codesign subsystem to lock _CodeSignature/*, preventing in-place re-signing
140:     even by the owner. Copying to /tmp gives us unconditional ownership of the
141:     inodes, so xattr and codesign always succeed there.
142:     """
143:     temp_app = Path(tempfile.mkdtemp()) / app_path.name
144:     shutil.copytree(app_path, temp_app)
145:     # Strip provenance from the copy (succeeds because we own it).
146:     subprocess.call(['xattr', '-dr', 'com.apple.provenance', os.fspath(temp_app)],
147:                     stderr=subprocess.DEVNULL)
148:     # Re-sign ad-hoc to drop Qt's Library Validation entitlement, which would
149:     # cause macOS to SIGKILL Designer when DYLD_INSERT_LIBRARIES injects
150:     # libpython (not signed by Qt). Safe because Designer has no network access;
151:     # the only remaining risk is a compromised libpython on disk, which is a
152:     # general risk for any Python package and cannot be mitigated here.
153:     subprocess.call(['codesign', '--force', '--deep', '--sign', '-',
154:                      os.fspath(temp_app)], stderr=subprocess.DEVNULL)
155:     return temp_app / 'Contents' / 'MacOS' / app_path.stem
